text: Hello everyone. Ladies and gentlemen,
for the first time, we have an
admission from the mayor of Tehran
regarding the risk of an internal
collapse of the Islamic Republic regime
. Thus, with the sanctions imposed by
the U.S., Iran can no longer hold out.
In addition, Israel is dismantling what
is known as the Axis of Resistance.
Hezbollah, their most important
stronghold, has been decimated by
Israel. As for Hamas, its leader has
just been captured alive by Israel.
Meanwhile, the Houthi forces are being
wiped out by government troops.
Consequently, the Axis of Resistance
that Iran has painstakingly built over
the past 50 years is collapsing right
before our eyes. This comes as no
surprise, as extremist clerics preach
about holy war and martyrdom while
living lives of extreme luxury
themselves. For example, look at
Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi; he has
taken two wives, and his second wife is
30 years younger than him. Abbas
Araghchi is about 62 years old this
year, while his wife is only about 32.
While he urges IRGC soldiers—the
Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps—to
fight and become martyrs to meet 72
virgins, his wife wears a headscarf,
just that one headscarf alone. It costs
as much as 500 US dollars. 500 US
dollars nowadays can be exchanged for a
kilogram of cash, a table full of money
. Just the other day, I sent you a
video showing 300 dollars being
exchanged for a table packed with money
. Therefore, the collapse of the
Islamic Republic of Iran's regime is
not surprising to us at all. And today,
the mayor of the capital, Tehran, Ali
Reza Zakani, spoke up. He stated that
we must address the serious failures
within the country. He warned that if
not, the country of Iran could collapse
from within. His exact words were that
resistance does not mean we should
ignore our internal problems. He
acknowledged problems across the
country, such as economic,
socio-political, and cultural issues in
Iran, especially the state of inflation
, the devaluation of the rial, and
severe fluctuations in exchange rates.
Along with the weakening and risk of
collapse of Iran is the weakening of
the entire Axis of Resistance led by
Hezbollah. We have analysis from
military analysts in the Middle East.
They say that over the past 50 years,
Iran has built a ring of fire around
Israel. The jewel in Iran's crown is
Hezbollah. The jewel in Hezbollah's own
crown is the complex they dug deep into
the Ali al-Tahir mountains, which the
Israel Defense Forces (IDF) just
captured the other day. Ladies and
gentlemen, on the 4th, this command
complex fell into the hands of the
Israel Defense Forces (IDF). It was
built over the past 20 years with
Iran's help and at a massive cost. This
base includes command and control rooms
, including weapons and supply depots,
along with field medical stations. All
were buried deep, from 30 to 50 meters
into solid rock. It is only 10 km from
the Israeli border. This is where
Hezbollah planned to coordinate their
own attacks alongside Hamas. However,
the Israel Defense Forces first reached
this mountain on the 31st, and by June
12th, the Israeli field division had
captured the main part of the mountain.
Following that, Israel began to lay
siege. They shot down every attempt at
reinforcement, including intruders and
supply drones. And then Israel
escalated, pushing their own drones
into the tunnels and using loudspeakers
continuously day and night. Throughout
the summer, Iranian and Hezbollah
forces were surrounded. The enemy
forces below began to surrender. Some
retreated, some were eliminated,
allowing the Israel Defense Forces (IDF
) to completely isolate the unit. In
mid-August, Iran warned Washington that
a full-scale Israeli attack on the Ali
al-Tahir hill would lead to a
large-scale response. Because at that
time, more than a dozen officers of the
Iranian Islamic Revolutionary Guard
Corps (IRGC) were on the hill. Three
officials told Reuters that, including
at least two high-ranking officers.
However, in the attacks on the 3rd and
4th of the month, the Israel Defense
Forces (IDF) eliminated all IRGC
intelligence officers along with senior
Hezbollah commanders inside that
complex. Thus, this fortress has now
fallen. Iran has repeatedly threatened
retaliation, and in reality, Tehran has
had opportunities to escalate
significantly in recent weeks. But they
have refused all of them. This proves
that Iran's potential is no longer
there. And this is also the first time
that Dany has witnessed the Wall Street
Journal. They have to admit that Iran
is currently losing. In their latest
editorial, the Wall Street Journal
stated that previously, both sides—
the US and Iran—believed they could
outlast the other and that time would
bring them the advantage. However,
recent developments show that the
balance is gradually shifting in favor
of the US and to the detriment of Iran.
Specifically, satellite images recorded
17 ship-to-ship transfers in the Gulf
of Oman in just one day. This proves
that Iran has lost control of the
Strait of Hormuz. The maritime tracking
organization TankerTrackers identified
the oil transfers on the 4th and
estimated the volume of oil transferred
at at least 24 million barrels. With
many other oil tankers looking for
partners, the oil transfer area is
gradually running out of space.
Additionally, the maritime tracking
organization also detected another 7.24
million barrels of oil and two LNG
carriers preparing to cross the Strait
of Hormuz under the protection of
CENTCOM, the US Central Command. Thus,
oil tankers will no longer have to pass
through the Strait of Hormuz to reach
ports in the Gulf. Therefore, oil will
be transported to the safer side of the
Strait of Hormuz and transferred on the
open sea, ship by ship, without Iran
being able to do anything. So, in the
current situation, Tehran is facing two
difficult choices. Iranian leaders have
repeatedly declared it unacceptable for
Gulf Arab states to continue exporting
oil while Iran's trade activities
remain blockaded. Therefore, according
to Professor Valinas, an expert on the
Middle East, Iran currently has two
options. One is to concede and return
to negotiations. Secondly, escalating
militarily to break out of being
cornered. Mr. Nas believes the
potential for escalation may be higher
because Iran's leadership thinks that
even if they eventually have to return
to the negotiating table and make
concessions, increasing military
pressure beforehand will help them
reduce the number of conditions they
must accept. In short, Iran faces only
one of two final outcomes: either
surrender or collapse. Similarly,
Russian President Vladimir Putin is
also being pushed into that exact
situation. Many former allies and
partners were once very close to Mr.
Putin. Even India's Prime Minister
Narendra Modi has spoken up, asking Mr.
Putin to stop this war. Next, let's
compare the context of Iran and the
context of Russia; what are the
similarities and what are the
differences? Why are Mr. Putin's
friends starting to publicly pressure
him to end the war? Recent candid
remarks from the leaders of India and
Kazakhstan show a notable shift in
relations between Russia and its
long-standing partners. As the war in
Ukraine enters its fifth year, its
consequences are not only weighing
heavily on Russia but are also
increasingly affecting the economies
and interests of nations that maintain
close ties with Moscow. As we have
witnessed, at the summit in Kyrgyzstan
—the Shanghai Cooperation
Organization summit—Indian Prime
Minister Narendra Modi directly told
Russian President Vladimir Putin that
it is time to move from an endless war
to ending the conflict. This was the
first time Mr. Modi had issued such a
call. But just over a month earlier,
President Tokayev of Kazakhstan had
also delivered a similar message.
During a meeting with Mr. Putin in
Siberia, Mr. Tokayev said that the
nature of this conflict remains unclear
and too many young people have already
died; it is time to end the war. All of
this proves that as the war drags on
and economic interests are harmed, not
only the Russian people but even
Putin's long-time friends are beginning
to demand that he end the war. Perhaps
this is also the reason why President
Trump is pushing for negotiations, with
special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared
Kushner set to travel to Moscow and
Kyiv this weekend. However, analysts
suggest that despite Russia being
bogged down on the battlefield and
suffering over 40,000 casualties each
month for the last two months, Russian
President Vladimir Putin will not
accept a ceasefire agreement. So, how
will Ukraine's armed forces deal with
Russia if Mr. Putin does not accept
that? We all know that Ukrainian
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has
implemented many military reforms,
especially replacing the
Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces,
and the new leader has proven very
effective. The evidence is that he has
achieved many successes on the
battlefield. Specifically, on the 4th
of this month, the new
Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces
of Ukraine, Mykhailo Drapatiy. He
presented his vision for the future of
the Ukrainian military with a very
clear statement. My goal is to lead an
army capable of winning today's battles
while simultaneously building the
military force for tomorrow. Below is
the entire plan that Commander-in-Chief
Drapatiy just presented. He stated, "
The Supreme Commander-in-Chief of the
Armed Forces, President Zelenskyy of
Ukraine, along with the Minister of
Defense, have entrusted me with the
command of the Ukrainian army, that is,
the Armed Forces of Ukraine. I assume
this task with the awareness that the
next phase of the war requires us to do
much more." Leading the army to fight
in the current war while ensuring the
military becomes stronger after the war
. Thus, we must fight, progress, and
adapt every day, thereby securing our
advantage. Every decision made in
coordination with the Minister of
Defense must help the armed forces
become stronger. Every change we
implement must improve combat
effectiveness right in the ongoing war.
These are my principles for leading and
developing the armed forces during
wartime. They explain how I intend to
command the military, while defining
priority objectives and the guiding
requirements for my actions. These
principles do not replace existing
plans, strategies, or operations, but
define my vision, priorities, and
leadership principles as
Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces
of Ukraine. My goal is to lead an army
capable of winning today's battles
while simultaneously building a
military force for tomorrow. We cannot
choose between conducting the current
war and preparing for the war of the
future. To succeed, we must perform
both of those tasks in parallel. My
first and most important task is to
stabilize the frontline, bring new
combat capabilities into use, and
provide commanders with the necessary
resources and freedom of action to
defeat the enemy. In parallel, we must
build, train, and retain personnel,
provide the military with necessary
high-quality weapons and equipment, and
develop defense industrial capacity to
sustain a prolonged war, not just now,
but also in the future. My duty as
Commander-in-Chief is to execute the
strategic direction set by the Supreme
Commander-in-Chief, the President of
Ukraine, to make decisions that only
the Commander-in-Chief can make, and to
enable subordinates to accomplish their
missions. I will not directly command
every battle or every operation. I will
command through operational intent,
delegating authority where appropriate,
holding all levels accountable, and
expecting all commanders to take
initiative. My priorities are very
clear. Every decision I make and every
resource I allocate must be directed
toward achieving one or more of the
following goals. The first goal is to
stabilize the frontline, while
maintaining existing combat
capabilities and bringing new ones into
use. The goal is to seize the
initiative wherever possible, prevent
the enemy from achieving their
operational objectives, and better
protect our people, cities, villages,
and critical infrastructure from enemy
attacks. The second goal is to build a
balanced system for shaping and
managing the human resources of the
armed forces. We need to change and
develop the system for recruitment,
training, service, rotation, retention,
and discharge of military personnel.
This system must ensure the military
has sufficient personnel and maintains
combat readiness, while also taking
into account the needs of service
members and society. This goal includes
developing leadership capabilities
alongside systems for training,
management, and personnel utilization.
Our task is to create conditions that
make military service predictable, fair
, and professional. Personnel decisions
must be based on the needs of the
military, competence, and service
results. We must strengthen public
trust in the armed forces and learn
from the past when developing policies
for recruitment, service, and the
conclusion of service terms. My third
goal is to ensure unity of action. The
armed forces must become the center for
shaping military intent and
coordinating the use of military
capabilities; operations on land, in
the air, at sea, in cyberspace, and in
the cognitive domain must be unified
under a common intent, synchronized in
time, space, and resources, and
directed toward a common outcome. No
branch, service, or structure shall
place its own interests above the
overall results of the campaign and the
entire defense force. Leadership begins
with a sincere concern for those
entrusted to our care. The armed forces
cannot accomplish this mission alone.
We must work closely with the Ministry
of Defense, the Ministry of Veterans
Affairs, other government agencies,
local authorities, and volunteer and
civil society organizations. My fourth
goal is to accelerate the process of
adaptation and the adoption of
innovations. We must learn faster than
the enemy by quickly applying lessons
from the war, new technologies, and
more effective methods of conducting
combat operations. My fifth objective
is to reform the armed forces. While
fighting the war, we must work with the
Minister of Defense to modernize the
military. This work includes command
and control systems, organizational
structure, military doctrine,
professional military education,
training, personnel management, digital
and unmanned capabilities, operational
independence, logistics,
lessons-learned systems, command
culture, and other areas that determine
the future effectiveness of the
military and help build a stronger
force. Building stronger armed forces
is a vital requirement, not a task for
the post-war period. My sixth objective
is to implement the principles of
mission command and integrate the
capabilities of all components within
the armed forces. Mission command means
that superiors define the objectives to
be achieved and grant subordinates the
initiative to choose how to execute
them. We must empower subordinate
commanders with the necessary authority
, assign responsibilities, and
integrate capabilities across all
domains to enhance the speed and
effectiveness of operations. My seventh
objective is to take care of military
personnel, their families, and veterans
. While also honoring those who have
made the ultimate sacrifice. The eighth
objective is to maintain the trust of
the Ukrainian people and our
international partners. We must earn
and maintain this trust through
professional leadership, accountability
, responsible resource management, and
close cooperation with those who
support Ukraine. Because the trust of
the people and international partners
in the military is one of Ukraine's
greatest strategic advantages. I also
set requirements for leaders within the
armed forces. Leadership in wartime is
the ability to guide people to achieve
results under conditions of uncertainty
, high risk, and limited resources.
Every commander, regardless of rank or
position, is responsible for the lives
of their service members and helps
shape the Ukrainian people's trust in
the armed forces. Therefore, I require
every leader to adhere to certain
principles. These requirements are
non-negotiable and apply equally to
officers, non-commissioned officers,
and civilian personnel entrusted with
leadership responsibilities. Leaders of
the Ukrainian Armed Forces must tell
the truth. They must provide honest
assessments, dare to challenge
established notions, and never allow
optimism. Fear, or personal ambition,
to distort reality. Healthy
professional debate helps make
decisions better. Silence makes them
weaker. Every soldier must understand
the commander's intent, not just their
own specific task but also the broader
goals of the battle or campaign, and
then act accordingly. They must act
decisively within the scope of the
commander's intent, use their
capabilities, exploit enemy weaknesses,
and make timely decisions without
waiting for permission when the
situation demands. Similarly, leaders
must both accomplish the mission and
ensure combat capability, protecting
their personnel, weapons, equipment,
and the assets entrusted to them. They
must treat force protection as a
routine part of all operations, never
becoming complacent or accepting
unnecessary risks. They must care for
service members, their families, and
veterans. They must know their people
well, support their families, care for
the wounded, and honor those who have
sacrificed in a solemn manner. I repeat
once again, leadership begins with
genuine care for those entrusted to our
charge. They must train the next
generation of leaders by mentoring and
developing subordinates, delegating
authority to encourage independent
thinking, and preparing others to
assume higher responsibilities.
Military commanders must learn faster
than the enemy, conduct honest
post-mission evaluations, and openly
share the lessons learned. They must
innovate, encourage experimentation,
implement new technology, and create an
environment where good ideas can come
from any soldier, regardless of rank or
position. They must fight as a unified
force, integrating capabilities across
all operational domains and seeking
collaboration instead of just
protecting the interests of their own
service, branch, or unit. Because no
single service, branch, or brigade can
win on its own. Leaders must
communicate simply and clearly, issuing
concise, easy-to-understand orders that
define the mission, intent, and desired
outcomes, while granting subordinates
the freedom to choose how to complete
the task. They must reduce unnecessary
administrative procedures and ensure
every soldier understands the mission,
the commander's intent, and their role
in the execution process. Finally, unit
command must build disciplined,
professional teams and uphold the
highest standards of conduct in the
armed forces, where there is no place
for corruption, abuse of power,
harassment, discrimination, or
injustice. War inevitably involves
mistakes. A decision made in good faith
under uncertain circumstances is part
of war. But negligence and the
concealment of the truth are
unacceptable. The cost of a mistake is
the lives of our people. Therefore,
every mistake must be acknowledged,
investigated, analyzed honestly, and
used as a lesson to ensure it does not
happen again. As Commander-in-Chief, I
will require commanders and
headquarters at all levels to implement
this. We must speak the truth, trust
one another, constantly learn, and take
responsibility for our service. By
doing so, we will preserve the legacy
of our predecessors, continue to
deserve the trust of the Ukrainian
people and our partners, and pass on a
stronger armed force to the next
generation. We must achieve a lasting
and just peace, while building an army
strong enough for the future. No
aggressor has any reason to claim that
attacking Ukraine is an acceptable way
to achieve their own goals. Ladies and
gentlemen, we can see that Ukraine is
developing its military toward
transparency and professionalism in
line with NATO standards. In contrast,
the Russian military still retains its
Soviet-style structure and stagnation.
If this trend continues, which side
will victory belong to? I invite you to
help Dani by leaving your opinions in
the comments section below. I would
like to thank you and look forward to
seeing you in the next program. Thank
you all very much.
